title: Knowing How --- the Verb That Once Meant Taste

lessons.title: saber — the verb that started out meaning "to taste"
lessons.gloss: to know how — before an infinitive it names a skill you learned, where poder names a chance you happen to have

segments.text: Say I can read. (Puedo leer.) Hold that sentence — it means something narrower than you think.
poder — puedo, puedes, puede.
la sopa and el ajo — how this starts.
sa-BER, weight on the second beat. The b is soft — lips close but never quite meet. The final r is one tap. see pronunciation reference.
saber — "to know." That gloss is the end of the story; the beginning is better.
Latin sapere meant to taste, and Spanish still uses it that way daily:
Esta sopa sabe a ajo. — This soup tastes of garlic.
Not a second verb that looks the same. It is saber, doing its original job.

Tasting to knowing is one short step, and English takes it too: whoever can taste the difference can tell the difference. Say he has taste and you are not talking about his tongue. So the seam still shows — sabe a ajo, it tastes of garlic; sabe leer, he knows how to read.

English borrowed pieces of the family from Latin. Savour is sapor, "flavour," sapere's own noun. Insipid is in- plus sapidus, "tasty" — what is insipid has no sapor. And sapiens, the present participle, gave us Homo sapiens: read strictly, not the wise animal but the tasting one, the animal that tells things apart.

blocks.title: Grammar lens — saber plus an infinitive

segments.text: A plain infinitive straight after saber means know how to — a skill you were taught and still have.
Sé leer. — I know how to read. ¿Sabes escribir? — Do you know how to write?
Against the verb you already had:

utterances: Sé leer., I know how. I learned it.
Puedo leer., I am able to right now — there is light.

segments.text: Both come out as "I can read," and they are not interchangeable. Sé leer pero hoy no puedo is ordinary Spanish: the skill is permanent, the opportunity is not.
Two forms to start with. The yo form is irregular and very short:
sé — I know how.
sabes — you know how.
You can say what you know how to do, and ask someone else — and you know why the soup and the skill are one verb.

segments.instruction: sé leer pero hoy no puedo
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *sé leer pero hoy no puedo*]

segments.text: What did sapere mean first? (To taste.) Which is the learned skill, sé leer or puedo leer? (Sé leer.)

lessons.title: Review — the verbs that will not sit behind sé
lessons.gloss: put the verbs from the chapter before behind sé and behind puedo — two of them fit both, and two of them show you what saber actually means

segments.text: "I know how to throw." (Sé lanzar.)
You have saber plus a plain verb, and you have the four verbs from the chapter before. Put them together and something useful goes wrong.

utterances: lanzar. behind sé: sé lanzar — fine. behind puedo: puedo lanzar — fine.
borrar. behind sé: sé borrar — fine. behind puedo: puedo borrar — fine.
empujar. behind sé: sé empujar — odd. behind puedo: puedo empujar — fine.
gritar. behind sé: sé gritar — odd. behind puedo: puedo gritar — fine.

segments.text: All four go behind puedo without a blink. Only two go behind sé.
Saber before a plain verb does not mean "can." It means know how to — and knowing how is something you were once taught.

Throwing well is learned. Erasing properly is learned. But nobody was ever taught to shout, and nobody took lessons in pushing. So sé gritar lands strangely. It is not ungrammatical; it claims a skill where there is none.

That is the cleanest test there is for the difference you met with poder. Puedo gritar is ordinary: I am able to, right now, or I am allowed to. Swap in sé and the sentence quietly claims you studied it.
Sé nadar pero hoy no puedo. The skill is permanent; the chance is not.

And the root says the same thing from underneath. Saber is Latin sapere, "to taste" — and the one who can taste is the one who can tell things apart. Discrimination first, knowledge second. It is why the verb for having a flavour and the verb for having a skill are one verb in Spanish.

segments.instruction: sé lanzar, sé borrar, puedo empujar, puedo gritar

segments.prompt: Say you know how to throw.

feedback.correct: A skill, so saber takes it happily.

segments.prompt: Why does se gritar sound odd?
acceptedResponses: shouting is not a learned skill

feedback.correct: Saber claims you were taught it. Nobody was taught to shout.
feedback.incorrect: Because saber claims a learned skill, and shouting is not one.

segments.prompt: What did Latin sapere mean before it meant to know?

feedback.correct: The one who can taste is the one who can tell things apart.

segments.text: What does saber plus a plain verb claim? (That you learned it.) Which of the two is about the chance you happen to have? (Poder.) And what did sapere mean first? (To taste.)
